processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: The 5 kg vacuum-induction ingot was heated to 1100 °C for 2 h before forging (Fig. 1 plateau labelled 'Homogenization at 1100 °C for 2 h').
The ingot was forged into a square forging ingot measuring 80 mm × 70 mm.
After forging, the ingot was reheated to 1100 °C and held for 2 h preparatory to hot rolling.

processing_steps.temperature: initial rolling temperature approximately 1050 °C; finishing rolling temperature approximately 950 °C
processing_steps.reduction_ratio: hot rolled from 80 to 12 mm thickness (in eight passes)
processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Hot rolled from 80 to 12 mm thickness in eight passes, with initial rolling temperature ~1050 °C and finishing rolling temperature ~950 °C; thermomechanical rolling in the dual-phase region produced the laminated microstructure.
After hot rolling the plate was air cooled to room temperature and the corresponding sample was labelled HR. During cooling, austenite underwent ferrite and martensite transformation.

structures.overall_structure: Micro-laminated (banded) microstructure consisting of δ-ferrite (δ-F) bands and lath martensite (M) lamellar, produced by thermomechanical rolling in the dual-phase region; retained austenite (RA) observed in the martensite bands, and α-ferrite (α-F) also formed on cooling.

microstructure_list.region: overall bulk (through-thickness of the hot-rolled plate)

phases_present.morphology: small regions inside the martensite bands (more concentrated in HR than in QA specimens)

defects.lattice_distortion: HR shows the highest overall KAM (local misorientation) signal of the six conditions in Fig. 7(a-1)

interfaces.phase_evolution: During hot rolling in the dual-phase region a dual-phase layered microstructure of δ-ferrite and austenite formed; on cooling to room temperature the weakly stable austenite underwent martensitic transformation, giving α-ferrite and lath martensite, with retained austenite remaining in the martensite bands (Mf of the steel below room temperature).
interfaces.interface_notes: The report notes that hardness difference between δ-ferrite band and tempered-martensite lamellar leads to stress concentration at their interfaces; crack-related interface behaviour is described mainly for the annealed (QA) fracture surfaces, not measured separately on HR.

measurement_conditions.specimen_geometry: rod-shaped specimen, M10*60 mm, gauge length 25 mm; tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction of the hot-rolled plate
measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Tensile properties of the various treatment states measured at room temperature on a WDW-100E electronic tensile testing machine.

tensile_properties.stress_strain_curves: Engineering stress–strain curve of HR (Fig. 5a): highest tensile strength (~1107 MPa, ~1100 MPa) reached at only ~4–5 % strain, poor total elongation (~5.6 %).

comparative_performance.comparison_metric: The hot-rolled (HR) reference state provides the strongest but least ductile baseline: highest TS (~1107 MPa) and lowest PSE (6.2 ± 0.6 GPa %) among all studied states, used as the benchmark against which the intercritical quenching-annealing (QA) conditions are compared.

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Metallographic specimens mechanically polished (PG-1A polishing machine) and etched in 10 % nitric acid alcohol; room temperature.
characterization_methods.purpose: Observe and analyse the microstructure of the hot-rolled (HR) state.
characterization_methods.key_findings: HR shows a laminated microstructure of δ-ferrite (δ-F) bands alternating with lath martensite (M); α-ferrite (α-F) and M are visible at higher magnification and small retained austenite (RA) regions lie inside the martensite bands (Fig. 3a, b; 50 µm and 10 µm scale bars).

characterization_methods.instrument_or_setup: EBSD (Oxford Instruments) probe with FE-SEM; HKL Channel5 software and Python for data analysis.
characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Specimens electrochemically polished in electrolyte of 10 % perchloric acid, 5 % glycerol and 85 % ethyl alcohol (15~20 V, 0.8–1.2 A); EBSD step size 150 nm.
characterization_methods.purpose: Determine austenite distribution/band contrast, KAM maps, grain-boundary distribution and GND density of the HR specimen.
characterization_methods.key_findings: By EBSD the HR austenite volume fraction is ~16 %; austenite (red) is concentrated in patchy bands inside the martensitic regions; HR has the highest KAM signal of the six conditions and GND densities of 10.81 × 10^14 m^-2 (BCC) and 8.37 × 10^14 m^-2 (FCC).

characterization_methods.measurement_conditions: Room temperature, strain rate 0.375 min^-1; rod-shaped specimen M10*60 mm, gauge length 25 mm; tensile axis parallel to the rolling direction.
characterization_methods.purpose: Measure tensile properties (YS, TS, TE) of the HR state at room temperature.
characterization_methods.key_findings: HR: YS 305 ± 11 MPa, TS 1107 ± 32 MPa, TE 5.6 ± 0.4 %, yield-tensile ratio 0.28, PSE 6.2 ± 0.6 GPa % — highest strength but poorest ductility of all states.

computational_details.simulation_method: equilibrium thermodynamic (CALPHAD) phase-fraction and composition-partitioning calculation
computational_details.boundary_and_initial_conditions: Equilibrium calculation for the Fe–9Mn–5Al-0.3C (wt.%) steel over ~500–1600 °C (phase fractions) and ~500–1400 °C (Mn/Al/C mass fractions in ferrite and austenite).
computational_details.validation_against_experiment: Used to select the quenching and intercritical annealing temperatures; the calculated A1 (cementite precipitation) temperature of ~617 °C and the maximum austenite fraction (~91.4 % at ~970 °C) guided the experimental temperatures, with an acknowledged discrepancy of the software.

unmapped_findings: HR (hot-rolled) exhibited the highest tensile strength, 1107 ± 32 MPa, but poor ductility, 5.6 ± 0.4 %, attributed to its highest GND densities (BCC 10.81 × 10^14 m^-2, FCC 8.37 × 10^14 m^-2) arising from the relatively larger ferrite content (b0051).

In HR the retained austenite distribution is more concentrated (patchy bands within the martensitic regions) than in the QA specimens; the γ/α boundary density of IQ-1050 was higher than that of HR (b0031, b0059).
The Mf temperature of the experimental steel was lower than room temperature, as indicated by retained austenite observed in the martensite bands of the HR state (b0028).

HR showed the highest values of sub-block boundary density and of low-/high-angle packet boundary density among the conditions according to Fig. 8(b), whereas block boundary density of HR was lower than that of IQ-1050 (b0059, figure_008).
The steel density 7.34 g·cm^-3 (Archimedes drainage method), 6.7 % lower than low-carbon low-alloyed steels, applies to the whole experimental steel including the HR state (b0016).
